sections.h2: Which office values a Brownsville home and which one bills it?
sections.html:
Two county offices, easy to confuse. Cameron Appraisal District staff appraise the property from an office in San Benito, and the Cameron County Tax Assessor-Collector mails a single combined bill for the county, the school district, the cities and special districts. The appraisal district holds no tax amounts and accepts no payments.

Its website offers a property search, a map search and a Truth in Taxation portal. Brownsville owners pay no state property tax, since Texas does not levy one, so every rate on the bill traces to a local body.

sections.h2: What rates did Brownsville's taxing units list for 2026?
sections.html:
The county's Truth in Taxation summary prints a rate per $100 of taxable value for each unit that touches most Brownsville homes. The figures below set 2026 beside 2025.

Rates per $100 of taxable value, from the Cameron County Truth in Taxation summary

City of Brownsville$0.603504$0.603504
Brownsville ISD$0.771600$0.831460
Cameron County$0.424393$0.424393

Brownsville Navigation District$0.025589$0.025589

The city line splits into $0.353581 for maintenance and operations and $0.249923 for debt. Its no-new-revenue rate reads $0.563407 and its voter-approval rate $0.613440. The school district's line has fallen a long way from the $1.208690 it printed for 2022.

Drainage districts, municipal utility districts and other special districts add their own levy, so read every line on your bill. The city has also posted a notice of intent to issue certificates of obligation up to $27,000,000, to be paid from property tax and landfill surplus revenue, and it lists $355,576,000 in outstanding debt principal. Those debt numbers help explain the debt portion of the city rate.

sections.h2: What does a late Brownsville bill cost?
sections.html:
Payment is due January 31 on bills mailed around October 1. Starting February 1 the Comptroller says a six percent penalty plus one percent interest apply, and the county office summarizes that as seven percent.

  • Each month adds a point of penalty, topping out at 12 percent in July.
  • A taxing unit that brings in a collection lawyer can tack on as much as 20 percent.
  • Tax Code 33.011 lets an owner request a waiver, generally if payment comes within 21 days of learning the bill was late.

An owner who is elderly, disabled, or a disabled veteran or a veteran's surviving spouse, and who claims a homestead, can pay in four parts: January 31, March 31, May 31 and July 31. The office posts card and e-check fees, which are 3 percent for cards, $1.00 for an e-check of $5,000 or less and $3.00 above that.

sections.h2: Which exemptions matter most on a Brownsville homestead?
sections.html:
School taxes drop on the first $140,000 of a homestead's value, with $60,000 more off the school bill for an owner who is elderly or disabled. Appraised value of a homestead can climb only 10 percent a year.

The appraisal district says a school tax ceiling for a senior can follow the owner to another Texas homestead, though it rises after additions such as a pool, garage or room. An owner picks either over-65 or disabled status, not both, and each spouse files with proof of Texas residency.

A local layer is new. The Brownsville Navigation District, the Port of Brownsville, approved a full homestead exemption for qualifying owners who are elderly or disabled. The city's September 2026 notice says it starts with the 2027 tax year and covers Brownsville, Rancho Viejo, Los Fresnos, Indian Lake and Starbase. Disabled veterans may qualify for a partial exemption, and a 100 percent rating brings a full one. Forms go to the appraisal district by April 30, and Form 50-114 covers the homestead types.

sections.h2: How does the Cameron Appraisal District handle a protest?
sections.html:
A protest must be written. Mail it, deliver it, fax it to (956) 399-6969 or email protest@cameroncad.org. The mailing address is PO Box 1010, San Benito, TX 78586, and the postmark has to land inside the window: the later of May 15 and the thirtieth day after the value notice No official form is needed, only the owner, the property and a statement that you disagree.

  • Informal hearings with an appraiser: walk-ins run from April 14 to May 16, first come first served, and requested ones happen by phone.
  • Formal hearing: usually three members, about 15 minutes, with at least 15 days of notice.
  • One postponement is allowed without a showing of cause if you named no agent.
  • An appeal can go to district court, binding arbitration under limited conditions, or in Cameron County to the State Office of Administrative Hearings.

The board rules on January 1 market value only. Service quality and tax rates are outside its reach. Without a timely protest neither the appraiser nor the board can change the value. Every property is reappraised at least every third year, and a notice is not required when the increase is $1,000 or less.

sections.h2: What shaped Brownsville, and how many people live there?
sections.html:
Brownsville stands at the southern tip of Texas, facing Matamoros over the Rio Grande, and it seats Cameron County government. The Handbook of Texas traces the town to 1848, when Charles Stillman and a partner platted a townsite next to Fort Brown. County seat status followed on January 13, 1849. Voters created the Brownsville Navigation District in December 1928 to build the ship channel, and the port opened May 15, 1936. Texas Southmost College, which still levies, began partnering with the University of Texas at Brownsville in 1991.

  • Population: 192,957 in the 2025 estimate, a 3.6 percent rise since the 2020 count.
  • Middle owner-occupied home value: $139,900, pooled 2020 through 2024.
  • Owner-occupancy rate: 61.7 percent.
  • Typical rent of $923 and 3.13 people per household.
  • 131.53 square miles of land.

sections.h2: What else should a Brownsville seller know about records and tax?
sections.html:
A sale can fund with taxes owing, because the title company gets a payoff from the tax office and pays it. The January 1 owner remains personally liable for that year's bill even after a later sale.

Copies of deeds, plats and mortgage records come from the Cameron County Clerk at 835 E. Levee St., Brownsville, (956) 544-0815, not from the appraisal district. A change of ownership needs a recorded instrument or volume and page. Mobile homes need a Statement of Ownership and Location before the land and home combine on one bill. Land taken out of agricultural use triggers a rollback tax owed by whoever holds title then.

If a bill is already late, ask the Cameron tax office about a payment agreement. The Comptroller says some collectors allow up to 36 months and that a plan is required for a residence homestead. After a collection suit starts, court costs join the bill. Foreclosure sales are public auctions with no statewide list, so look for notices from the county clerk and tax office.

faqs.q: Which Brownsville taxing unit has the highest 2026 rate?
faqs.a: Brownsville ISD, at $0.771600 per $100 of taxable value, ahead of the city at $0.603504 and the county at $0.424393 in the county's summary table.

faqs.q: On what date is a Brownsville tax bill late?
faqs.a: February 1, for anything unpaid after January 31. Penalty and interest begin then, and the penalty reaches 12 percent on July 1.

faqs.q: Can I email a Brownsville appraisal protest?
faqs.a: Yes. The appraisal district accepts written protests by email at protest@cameroncad.org, by fax, by mail or by hand. Mailed protests must carry a postmark by the deadline.

faqs.q: Do older Brownsville homeowners get anything from the port district?
faqs.a: Yes, in one respect: the Brownsville Navigation District approved a full homestead exemption for owners who are elderly or disabled, beginning with the 2027 tax year. Apply through the appraisal district.

faqs.q: Which office holds my Brownsville deed?
faqs.a: The Cameron County Clerk, 835 E. Levee St., Brownsville, (956) 544-0815. The appraisal district keeps no deeds.
